title: Algebraic closure is necessary: the Nullstellensatz fails over ℝ
content: The docstring frames the entry as a counterexample answering the parent's open questions (can the IsAlgClosed hypothesis be dropped?). The parent proves the strong form vanishingIdeal(zeroLocus I) = √I and weak form (I ≠ ⊤ ⟹ zeroLocus nonempty) over an algebraically closed field. This file exhibits the single ideal J = (X² + 1) in ℝ[X] that is proper yet has empty real zero locus — so both forms fail — while the same ideal over ℂ has a nonempty zero locus (witness i). The contrast pinpoints algebraic closure as exactly the hypothesis the Nullstellensatz requires: no more, no less.
mathContext: Weak Nullstellensatz over alg. closed $k$: $I\neq\top\Rightarrow V(I)\neq\emptyset$. Over $\mathbb{R}$, $J=(X^2+1)$ is proper but $V_{\mathbb{R}}(J)=\emptyset$; over $\mathbb{C}$, $i\in V_{\mathbb{C}}(J)$.

title: The witness ideal J = (X² + 1) over ℝ
content: Jreal is the principal ideal generated by X₀² + 1 in the one-variable polynomial ring MvPolynomial (Fin 1) ℝ (using MvPolynomial for compatibility with the parent's zeroLocus / vanishingIdeal API). The helper aeval_gen_real records that evaluating the generator at a real point x gives x₀² + 1 — the quantity whose strict positivity is the whole obstruction.

title: Empty real zero locus: x² + 1 > 0
content: zeroLocus_real_empty shows V_ℝ(Jreal) = ∅. Any point x in the zero locus would force the generator (which is in Jreal by subset_span) to vanish, i.e. x₀² + 1 = 0; but nlinarith with sq_nonneg (x 0) refutes this since x₀² + 1 ≥ 1 > 0. The positivity of x² + 1 over ℝ is the concrete reason the real variety is empty — the polynomial has no real root.

title: The ideal is proper — and ℂ is what proves it
content: Jreal_ne_top proves 1 ∉ Jreal, so the ideal is proper. The elegant trick: if 1 = c·(X² + 1) for some c, apply the ℝ-algebra homomorphism aeval(i) : ℝ[X] → ℂ sending X ↦ i. The generator maps to i² + 1 = 0 (Complex.I_sq), so the right side becomes 0 while the left stays 1, giving 1 = 0 in ℂ — absurd. This is precisely where the missing complex root i enters: ℂ certifies that the ℝ-ideal is proper even though it has no real zeros.
mathContext: If $1 = c(X^2+1)$ then $\mathrm{aeval}_i$ gives $1 = c(i)\cdot(i^2+1) = 0$ in $\mathbb{C}$, contradiction. So $J_{\mathbb{R}}\neq\top$.

title: Both weak and strong Nullstellensatz fail over ℝ
content: Two failure theorems combine the previous facts. weak_nullstellensatz_fails_over_real packages Jreal ≠ ⊤ with V_ℝ(Jreal) not nonempty — directly contradicting the weak conclusion that a proper ideal has a common zero. strong_nullstellensatz_fails_over_real shows vanishingIdeal(V_ℝ(Jreal)) = vanishingIdeal(∅) = ⊤, while Jreal.radical ≠ ⊤ (since radical = ⊤ ⟺ ideal = ⊤, and Jreal is proper), so the identity I(V(J)) = √J breaks. Both failures are pure consequences of 'proper ideal, empty variety' — impossible over an algebraically closed field.

title: Positive contrast: over ℂ the zero locus is nonempty
content: Jcomplex is the same ideal (X² + 1) but over ℂ. zeroLocus_complex_nonempty exhibits x₀ = i as a common zero: any element of the ideal is c·(X² + 1), which evaluates at i to c(i)·(i² + 1) = 0 (Complex.I_sq). So the very root ℝ lacked makes the Nullstellensatz hold over the algebraic closure. Placed beside the ℝ failures, this isolates IsAlgClosed as the exact, tight hypothesis — answering the parent's open question.
mathContext: Over $\mathbb{C}$: $i^2 + 1 = 0$, so $i\in V_{\mathbb{C}}(J)\neq\emptyset$ — the Nullstellensatz is restored exactly by passing to the algebraic closure.
prerequisites: ℂ as algebraic closure of ℝ
